method: Rounding runs on a grid anchored at midnight, so a clock time is moved to the nearest, the previous or the next multiple of the chosen increment and every policy lands on the same minute values whatever the date. The increments are 1, 5, 6, 10 and 15 minutes: 5 minutes, one-tenth of an hour and quarter of an hour are the steps the regulation names, and 1 minute turns rounding off. Nearest takes the closer grid line and breaks an exact tie upward, so 09:03 rounds up to 09:06 at a 6-minute increment and 09:05 to 09:10 at 10 minutes. Down floors to the line at or before the punch and up raises to the line at or after it. In punch mode each clock-in and clock-out is rounded first and the payable time is the difference between the two rounded readings, which is how a time-and-attendance system works; in duration mode the shift length is computed from the raw punches and then rounded. A clock-out earlier than the clock-in is read as the next day and 1,440 minutes are added, so an overnight shift can be entered in one row; a row whose two times are equal is refused because a 24-hour shift and a zero-length shift cannot be told apart. Times are whole minutes, HH:MM, with no seconds, and up to 30 rows are analysed at once. Totals carry the recorded minutes, the payable minutes, their signed difference and payable hours rounded to two decimals. The page rounds hours only: it does not compute pay, overtime, premiums or legal compliance, and rounding is acceptable only where it averages out over time and does not leave worked time uncompensated.

sources.title: 29 CFR 785.48 - Use of time clocks: rounding starting and stopping time to the nearest 5 minutes, one-tenth or quarter of an hour
